blocks.script:
Donald Trump escalated the trade war with Canada again, and it's the story dominating Ottawa this week. Hours after Canada's retaliatory tariffs on 28 billion dollars of American goods took effect Tuesday, the president signed proclamations banning imports of Canadian alcohol, including beer, wine and rye whisky, along with motorcycles over 800 cubic centimetres, whey protein and molasses. He's also imposing 50 percent tariffs on a separate list: cheese, motorboats, paper products, aluminum goods, furniture and lamps, while lifting tariffs on a handful of items like cement and toilet paper.

For Manitoba that matters directly. The province's distillers, brewers and dairy processors sell into that American market, and manufacturers supplying auto and aerospace parts are watching the broader tariff list closely.

Ottawa's response has been measured so far. Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc says the government is assessing the move and remains in contact with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. Greer himself told the Financial Times he finds Canada's posture "unhinged", a line getting a lot of play in Ottawa this week. Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed Canadians directly in an online video, warning that "this won't be easy and I won't pretend otherwise." A Nanos Research poll done for the Globe and Mail found 80 percent of Canadians support or somewhat support Ottawa's dollar for dollar countertariffs, so there's real public backing for the hard line even as businesses brace for higher costs.

Carney is currently at a two day cabinet retreat in Banff, where ministers are being asked to show progress against the government's seven stated priorities, top of the list being a new economic and security relationship with the United States. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy joined Carney in Calgary for a signing ceremony before the retreat began. Separately, Ottawa quietly streamlined environmental approvals for pipelines and transmission lines this week, a move widely read as an olive branch to Alberta Premier Danielle Smith. On that note, Alberta has a referendum question this fall that could open the door to eventual separation, and CBC reports the campaign trying to keep the province in Canada is underfunded and struggling to organize.

Parliament itself stays adjourned until September 21st, and that's drawing criticism. One Globe and Mail opinion piece argues that with tens of billions in trade at stake, the House should be sitting now rather than waiting. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is pressing that case from New York this week, though CBC also reports his own caucus is showing signs of friction over how hard to push the trade file. On the smaller party side, the Green Party leadership race is down to one candidate, former MP Mike Morrice, after his only rival withdrew.

On the Bank of Canada, which is on your watch list: it held its policy rate at 2 and a quarter percent on September 2nd, a seventh consecutive hold, citing Middle East driven energy prices and the fluid trade situation with Washington. The next decision lands October 28th, and most bank economists now expect the next move, whenever it comes, to be a hike rather than a cut.

Here at home, the Manitoba legislature is still on summer break. It reconvenes September 29th, a week after Parliament. In the meantime, Premier Wab Kinew's government has been governing by news release, this week unveiling a Net Zero Action Plan with 90 specific actions toward 2050, alongside new housing investment and a defence alliance announcement. Watch for how the province positions itself on trade retaliation and interprovincial trade barriers once the House returns, since that's shaping up as a fall theme across the country.

blocks.title: OpenAI's Math Claim, Agents, and Canadian Capital
blocks.script:
The biggest story in tech right now is a fight over a math proof, and it matters more than it sounds. OpenAI says an internal, unreleased model directed ten thousand coordinating agents to crack the Navier-Stokes equations, one of the six unsolved Millennium Prize Problems, in eighty-eight hours. That's a two-hundred-year-old puzzle about whether fluid motion can break down mathematically. Quanta Magazine reports the result was checked in the formal language Lean, so mathematicians are confident it's correct. The catch: a New York University professor named Tristan Buckmaster says he and an Anthropic researcher were close to a related result themselves, and that OpenAI moved fast right after hearing rumors of their work. OpenAI, per its own release, says the effort began September 1st after hearing that rumor. Nobody is accusing anyone of theft outright, but for you, the takeaway is this: frontier labs are now racing each other using signals from each other's users, and if your clients or their businesses use these tools for anything proprietary, the privacy settings matter more than they think.

That race is also splitting the safety camp. TechCrunch reports an Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, quit this week, calling the competition between Anthropic and OpenAI "gambling with our lives" and pushing for pacing agreements between labs. Meanwhile OpenAI just added Paul Christiano, a well-known alignment researcher, to its nonprofit board. So one lab is losing a safety voice publicly, the other is adding one. Worth knowing if clients ask whether these companies are self-regulating.

On the enterprise side, agentic tools are now a security category of their own. TechCrunch reports Sequoia is doubling down on a startup called Cymphony, which gives security teams a single view of employees, AI agents, and other so-called nonhuman identities, tracking what systems and data those agents can touch. If a client runs a business that's plugged AI agents into email, scheduling, or payments, that's a real exposure point now, not a hypothetical one.

There's a productivity wrinkle too. TechCrunch reports AI spending per employee actually slumped at top firms in August, with falling token costs and cheaper models part of the story. That's a useful data point if clients ask whether AI capital spending is paying off yet. It's not a clean story of runaway adoption.

On the Canadian side, BetaKit reports RBC has launched a billion-dollar fund aimed at scaling homegrown tech companies, and Ottawa has unveiled a national AI literacy initiative delivered through the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute. The TSX30 list of top-performing Canadian tech stocks this year leans hardware: Celestica, MDA Space, and Telesat, with software names notably absent. And Clay, a Canadian-founded go-to-market startup, just raised one hundred fifteen million US dollars at a seven-billion-dollar valuation.

On the macro side, the Bank of Canada held its rate at two and a quarter percent on September 2nd, its seventh straight hold, citing Middle East-driven energy prices and new US tariffs. That one's on your watch list, worth flagging in any client conversation about rate direction.

Last, Google is putting thirteen billion euros into a single data center project in Finland, its largest single investment in Europe, a reminder that AI infrastructure spending abroad shows no sign of slowing even as adoption numbers at home look shakier.

blocks.title: Lifting Two Hours a Week Cuts Death Risk
blocks.script:
A new analysis from Harvard's T.H. Chan School of Public Health gives you an actual dose to point to if you train with weights. The study, published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, followed more than 147,000 adults for up to 30 years, pulling from three long running cohorts including the Health Professionals Follow-up Study and the two Nurses' Health Studies. Roughly 90 to 120 minutes of strength training per week was linked with a 13% reduced risk of premature death. Adding aerobic exercise to the weekly mix increased the longevity benefit further. This is observational, so it shows association, not proof that the lifting itself causes the effect, and self-reported activity over decades always has some noise in it. But the sample size and the three decade follow-up make it one of the sturdier pieces of evidence connecting resistance training to lifespan, not just to muscle and bone. If you're already training, the practical takeaway is that two solid sessions a week appears to capture most of the benefit, more isn't obviously better on the mortality curve.

On the Canadian health system side, Alberta is pushing to let physicians see private pay patients alongside public ones, and Ottawa is pushing back. Alberta's hospitals and surgical services minister defends the provincial jurisdiction, while the federal health minister raises concerns about compliance with the Canada Health Act. Commentary in The Hub argues physicians in Alberta, and most of Canada, are already able to opt out of the public system, and allowing them to practice privately without sacrificing their public role is a common-sense approach. Worth watching if clients ask about private care options, because however this lands could shape mixed public private billing well beyond Alberta.

Separately, CBC reports Bangladesh is facing its worst measles outbreak on record, with around 1,000 suspected and confirmed measles-related deaths reported since March, and hospitals struggling with overcrowding and shortages. It's a stark reminder of how fast a vaccine preventable disease comes back once coverage gaps open up, and it's a useful data point if the topic of childhood vaccination rates comes up with clients who have young kids.

None of today's items touch the Bank of Canada, Manitoba Hydro, or the local sports franchises, so nothing from the watch list to flag this time.

blocks.title: Canada Child Benefit Rises, New Paediatric Guidance Lands
blocks.script:
The Canada Child Benefit went up this summer, and it is worth mentioning to any client with young kids. Households can now receive up to $8,157 a year for a child under six and $6,883 a year for a child aged six to seventeen, paid monthly and tax free. That is an increase of up to $160 per child under six and up to $135 per child aged six to seventeen compared to last year, part of an annual two percent inflation adjustment. Families with net income under $38,237 get the full amount, and it is reduced for households above that threshold. A couple earning $65,000 with a five and a nine year old will receive about $11,430 this benefit year, nearly $400 more than last year. Because the payment is tax free, it can go straight into a Registered Education Savings Plan contribution without pushing anyone into a different bracket.

On the health side, the Canadian Paediatric Society posted new national guidance in June on injury prevention in children and youth, framed around prevention across the home and the car. It also issued updated flu vaccine recommendations for the 2026 to 2027 season in mid August, useful context if a client asks about daycare or school timing this fall.

On feeding, the standing guidance is to introduce foods that commonly cause allergy around six months of age and keep feeding them regularly. For infants at high risk of allergy, introduction can start earlier, but not before four months. That timing has not shifted, but it remains the most common question from new parents.

No changes to Employment Insurance parental leave this week. Standard leave stays at up to forty weeks combined between parents at fifty five percent of earnings, with an extended, lower paid option running longer for families who need more time.

blocks.title: Price to earnings: trailing, forward, and why both mislead in isolation / Questions that open: the difference between a good question and an interrogation
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Valuation reps, lesson 1: Price to earnings: trailing, forward, and why both mislead in isolation.

Nvidia's stock got hammered in early 2026 headlines for trading at what the Financial Times called a nosebleed valuation, then defended a week later for looking cheap. Same company, same week. The difference was which P/E ratio the writer picked.

Trailing price to earnings takes today's share price and divides it by the last twelve months of actual reported earnings per share. It is backward looking, it is audited, it is real. Forward P/E takes that same price and divides it by analysts' consensus estimate for the next twelve months of earnings. It is a guess, dressed up as a number.

Here is the worked example. Say a company trades at 120 dollars a share. Trailing earnings per share, from the last four quarters, is 3 dollars. Trailing P/E is 40. Analysts expect earnings to grow to 4.80 next year on new product demand. Forward P/E is 25. Same stock, same price, and one ratio says expensive, the other says reasonable. Neither is wrong. They are answering different questions.

The mistake people make is comparing one company's trailing P/E to another company's forward P/E, or worse, treating the forward number as fact instead of a consensus guess that gets revised every quarter, sometimes sharply, as Reuters has documented with semiconductor estimates through 2025.

What P/E reveals: how much the market is willing to pay today for a dollar of past or expected earnings, relative to peers. What it cannot reveal: whether that earnings number is clean, whether debt is funding the growth, or whether the estimate behind the forward figure has any discipline behind it. That is exactly why P/E sits inside your analysis step, before you ever touch a chart, and why you check it against the sector average, not in isolation.

In Thomson ONE, pull both from the same screen, the estimates tab under company overview shows trailing P/E and consensus forward P/E side by side, along with the number of analysts contributing to that estimate.

Communication, lesson 2: Questions that open: the difference between a good question and an interrogation.

Neil Rackham spent twelve years studying more than 35,000 sales calls across 23 countries, work that became the book SPIN Selling. He found something specific. The top performers did not ask more questions overall. They asked roughly four times as many open questions in the first ten minutes as average performers, and almost none of those were what he called implication questions, the kind that make someone defend a decision they already made.

That is the line between a good question and an interrogation. A good question invites the other person to think out loud with you. An interrogation asks them to justify something.

Here is the worked example. A client says, "We spent 40,000 dollars on a rebrand last year and our lead volume did not move." Interrogation: "Why did you spend 40,000 dollars if it did not work?" There is a verdict built into that question before the client even answers. Open version: "What were you hoping that 40,000 dollars would change, and what actually changed instead?" Same number, same fact, completely different posture. One asks them to defend. The other asks them to notice.

The mistake almost everyone makes is stacking two or three questions in a row without waiting. You ask, get half an answer, then jump in again because silence feels uncomfortable. Rackham's data showed the best performers left three to five seconds after a question before speaking again. That gap is where the real answer usually shows up.

lessons.label: Company & Economy Analysis
lessons.title: Price to earnings: trailing, forward, and why both mislead in isolation
lessons.script:
Nvidia's stock got hammered in early 2026 headlines for trading at what the Financial Times called a nosebleed valuation, then defended a week later for looking cheap. Same company, same week. The difference was which P/E ratio the writer picked.

Trailing price to earnings takes today's share price and divides it by the last twelve months of actual reported earnings per share. It is backward looking, it is audited, it is real. Forward P/E takes that same price and divides it by analysts' consensus estimate for the next twelve months of earnings. It is a guess, dressed up as a number.

Here is the worked example. Say a company trades at 120 dollars a share. Trailing earnings per share, from the last four quarters, is 3 dollars. Trailing P/E is 40. Analysts expect earnings to grow to 4.80 next year on new product demand. Forward P/E is 25. Same stock, same price, and one ratio says expensive, the other says reasonable. Neither is wrong. They are answering different questions.

The mistake people make is comparing one company's trailing P/E to another company's forward P/E, or worse, treating the forward number as fact instead of a consensus guess that gets revised every quarter, sometimes sharply, as Reuters has documented with semiconductor estimates through 2025.

What P/E reveals: how much the market is willing to pay today for a dollar of past or expected earnings, relative to peers. What it cannot reveal: whether that earnings number is clean, whether debt is funding the growth, or whether the estimate behind the forward figure has any discipline behind it. That is exactly why P/E sits inside your analysis step, before you ever touch a chart, and why you check it against the sector average, not in isolation.

In Thomson ONE, pull both from the same screen, the estimates tab under company overview shows trailing P/E and consensus forward P/E side by side, along with the number of analysts contributing to that estimate.

lessons.label: Communication
lessons.title: Questions that open: the difference between a good question and an interrogation
lessons.script:
Neil Rackham spent twelve years studying more than 35,000 sales calls across 23 countries, work that became the book SPIN Selling. He found something specific. The top performers did not ask more questions overall. They asked roughly four times as many open questions in the first ten minutes as average performers, and almost none of those were what he called implication questions, the kind that make someone defend a decision they already made.

That is the line between a good question and an interrogation. A good question invites the other person to think out loud with you. An interrogation asks them to justify something.

Here is the worked example. A client says, "We spent 40,000 dollars on a rebrand last year and our lead volume did not move." Interrogation: "Why did you spend 40,000 dollars if it did not work?" There is a verdict built into that question before the client even answers. Open version: "What were you hoping that 40,000 dollars would change, and what actually changed instead?" Same number, same fact, completely different posture. One asks them to defend. The other asks them to notice.

The mistake almost everyone makes is stacking two or three questions in a row without waiting. You ask, get half an answer, then jump in again because silence feels uncomfortable. Rackham's data showed the best performers left three to five seconds after a question before speaking again. That gap is where the real answer usually shows up.
lessons.task: In your next client call, catch yourself before any question that starts with "why did you," and swap it in your head for "what were you hoping" before it leaves your mouth.
lessons.drill: Record a 5 minute conversation with a colleague about a recent decision they made. Afterward, count two things: how many of your questions started with "why did you" versus "what were you hoping" or "what happened," and how many seconds of silence you left after each question before you spoke again. Good looks like at least 4 out of 5 questions open ended, and at least 3 seconds of silence held after each one before you jump in.

blocks.title: Trade War Escalates as Oil Nears $100
blocks.script:
Good morning. Markets are digesting a rough combination this week: escalating Canada-U.S. trade tensions and a sharp jump in oil prices tied to violence in the Middle East.

Let's start with trade. Canada's retaliatory tariffs on roughly 28 billion dollars worth of American goods took effect this week, according to The Peak and The Globe and Mail's Before the Bell newsletter. Nearly 700 U.S. products are affected, with tariffs set at 15, 25 or 50 percent. Industrial goods like aluminum, steel, cardboard and screws are hit hardest, though some consumer goods including clothing, furniture, dairy and cosmetics are also on the list.

The Peak reports that U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has confirmed Washington plans to add further tariffs on Canadian goods this week, potentially including outright import bans. President Trump has also been active on social media, complaining about the Canadian dollar, threatening to ban U.S. sales of Bombardier jets, and posting an AI-generated image referring to Prime Minister Mark Carney as "Governor." Bombardier shares fell after the threat, according to Globe and Mail reporting.

Prime Minister Carney addressed the nation as the tariffs took effect, warning Canadians that pivoting away from the United States will carry real costs, but arguing the alternative would be worse, per Globe and Mail coverage. The Peak notes that, so far, public opinion appears to back a firm stance, with 76 percent of Canadians saying the country did the right thing by walking away from trade talks last month. Whether that support holds as economic costs mount remains an open question.

Turning to oil, Brent crude pushed toward the 100 dollar a barrel mark this week, its highest level in roughly six weeks, according to Bloomberg's Markets Daily and The Globe's Before the Bell. West Texas Intermediate traded near 94 dollars. The move follows a serious escalation in the Middle East, with the U.S. and Iran trading attacks around the Strait of Hormuz and reports of strikes on energy facilities in Saudi Arabia. Iran has also threatened what it called economic warfare against the United States.

Analysts quoted by The Globe say the rally reflects both genuine tightness in tanker flows through Hormuz and a hefty geopolitical risk premium. Some of that pressure eased slightly after Iran signaled it was close to a deal with Oman on managing shipping through the strait, but analysts caution oil is likely to stay elevated as long as the strait remains contested.

Gold, often a safe haven in times like these, actually slipped, with spot prices down around 0.3 percent, according to Before the Bell. Copper, meanwhile, hit a record high, driven by supply tightness outside the U.S. as tariff-related buying pulls metal toward American markets, Globe and Mail reporting shows.

The commodity spike is feeding into a broader story about interest rates and volatility. Bloomberg's Markets Daily reports that strategists are bracing for a choppy autumn, citing rising rates expectations, fiscal deficit worries in the UK and France, the Israel-Iran conflict, and the run-up to U.S. midterm elections. One bond strategist quoted in the newsletter summed up the mood bluntly, saying volatility is probably the only certainty given the mix of Trump-driven trade policy and oil market swings.

Deutsche Bank strategist Henry Allen argued in a note cited by Bloomberg that markets may be underestimating how much central banks will ultimately need to raise rates, given that inflation isn't cooling as quickly as hoped. That tension will be tested with a widely expected quarter point hike from the European Central Bank, and possible moves from the Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan in the weeks ahead.

Bond markets are already feeling the strain. The U.S. 10 year Treasury yield sat near 4.8 percent, and Bloomberg reports it's shaping up to be one of the busiest weeks of the year for corporate debt issuance, much of it tied to financing the ongoing AI buildout.

Currency markets saw their own drama. The Japanese yen surged toward its strongest level of the year against the dollar, breaking through the 155 level before easing, according to Bloomberg. The move triggered a wave of stop losses and forced investors to unwind an estimated 2.35 trillion dollars in yen funded carry trades. Japan's finance minister said the country's currency policy hasn't changed, but the bigger worry flagged by Bloomberg is that continued yen strength could push U.S. borrowing costs higher and fuel demand for havens like gold and Bitcoin.

On individual stocks, Novartis shares slumped 10 percent after the Swiss drugmaker suffered its third clinical trial setback in a week, according to Bloomberg and Globe and Mail reporting, dragging down other biotech names including Ionis Pharmaceuticals, Dyne Therapeutics and Sarepta Therapeutics.

In broader market moves reported by The Globe, global stocks were mostly lower as the oil spike and trade tensions weighed on sentiment. Japan's Nikkei closed down 1.7 percent, Hong Kong's Hang Seng slipped, and European indexes were mixed but mostly softer. The Canadian dollar actually strengthened against its U.S. counterpart despite the tariff fight, trading in the 72 cent range and up close to 1 percent over the past month.

Elsewhere in economic news, Alberta based Tamarack Valley and Headwater agreed to a 10 billion dollar merger creating a major oil producer in the province's Clearwater region, according to Globe and Mail reporting. Enbridge announced a leadership change, with CEO Greg Ebel set to retire and Michele Harradence named as his successor. And Bank of Montreal became the first of Canada's Big Five banks to eliminate most online trading commissions, a move reportedly aimed at younger, cost sensitive investors.
talkingPoints: One: Canada's counter tariffs on roughly 28 billion dollars in U.S. goods are now in effect, with Washington signaling more tariffs, and possibly import bans, are coming this week.
Two: Oil prices are near six week highs and flirting with 100 dollars a barrel as attacks around the Strait of Hormuz and on Saudi energy facilities raise fears of supply disruption.
Three: Strategists are warning of a volatile autumn ahead, driven by central bank rate decisions, fiscal worries in Europe, elections, and a surge in corporate bond issuance tied to AI spending.
Four: The Japanese yen's sharp rally is forcing investors to unwind massive carry trades, a shift that could ripple into Treasury yields and global risk appetite.
Five: Copper hit a record high on tight supply, while gold slipped and Novartis shares tumbled 10 percent on repeated clinical trial failures.

blocks.title: Trade War Escalates as Oil Tops $100 a Barrel
blocks.script:
Good evening. Tonight we lead with the widening trade fight between Canada and the United States, a fresh spike in oil prices tied to the conflict between the U.S. and Iran, and a breakthrough for Germany's far right.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs on roughly 28 billion dollars worth of American goods took effect this week, hitting nearly 700 products with duties of 15, 25 or 50 percent. Industrial goods like aluminum, steel and cardboard took the biggest hit, though clothing, furniture, dairy and cosmetics from the U.S. were also affected, according to The Peak.

The Trump administration answered almost immediately. President Trump signed a series of executive orders banning imports of Canadian dairy products and most alcoholic drinks, including beer, wine and liquor, along with whey products, motorcycles and molasses, according to CBC News as reported by The Peak. New tariffs of 50 percent were also slapped on additional goods, and the president threatened to bar Canadian companies from selling to U.S. government contractors and to ban the sale of Bombardier jets in America, Bloomberg reports. Bombardier pushed back by pointing to its extensive U.S. manufacturing footprint.

Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the nation, warning Canadians that the country's pivot away from the United States will come at a cost, but arguing the alternative would be worse, according to the Globe and Mail. Polling cited by The Peak suggests most Canadians still back the tougher stance, with 76 percent saying Canada did the right thing by walking away from talks last month.

At the same time, Canada is looking to Europe. Bloomberg reports that Canada and the European Union are preparing to unveil a sweeping new partnership as soon as next week, covering trade and security, with both sides trying to get as close as legally possible without Canada joining the bloc outright. The EU's ambassador to Canada told the Toronto Star the relationship may need an entirely new name, since no existing model fits what they're building.

Turning to the Middle East, oil prices pushed past 100 dollars a barrel for the first time since July, according to Bloomberg, as the United States and Iran continued trading attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia said operations at several energy facilities were halted after strikes, and Yemen's Houthi rebels hit four Saudi cities with drones and missiles targeting oil sites, according to Reuters. The U.S. reportedly destroyed five Iranian tankers after Iran tried to strike a Navy warship, and Washington has moved to sanction Iran's airlines as part of a broader pressure campaign.

In German politics, the far right Alternative for Germany party won nearly 44 percent of the vote in a regional election in Saxony-Anhalt, according to the Guardian, giving it the most seats in that province's parliament. If the party forms government there, it would mark the first time since 1945 that the far right has held power in Germany, breaking through the political firewall mainstream parties had maintained against it.

In markets, both Canadian and American stocks fell through the week as commodity prices climbed and investors weighed the prospect of central banks having to keep interest rates higher for longer. Bloomberg's Deutsche Bank sourcing suggests strategists believe markets are underestimating how much tightening may still be needed given persistent inflation pressure. The Japanese yen has also been strengthening sharply, nearing its best levels of the year, which Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent addressed directly, saying he has strong insight into Bank of Japan policy and telling traders they can bet against him if they want.

In corporate news, Swiss drugmaker Novartis saw shares slump 10 percent after a third clinical trial setback in a week, according to the Globe and Mail, dragging down partner Ionis Pharmaceuticals and other biotech names. Saudi-backed golf league LIV Golf filed for bankruptcy, according to Bloomberg, with the Public Investment Fund agreeing to provide continued financing. Qualcomm struck a major chip deal with Amazon that could see Amazon buy up to 60 billion dollars in AI data center chips, according to the Globe and Mail. And Enbridge announced Michele Harradence will succeed Greg Ebel as chief executive.

Apple unveiled its long anticipated foldable iPhone this week, priced near 2,000 dollars, as new CEO John Ternus faces pressure to prove the company can keep pace on artificial intelligence after a summer stock surge that added an estimated 570 billion dollars in market value, Bloomberg reports.

In U.S. politics, Chris Pappas won New Hampshire's Democratic Senate primary, setting up a November race against Republican John Sununu in a state that hasn't elected a GOP senator in 16 years. Meanwhile the Justice Department is investigating admissions practices at elite public high schools including Stuyvesant in New York and Lowell in San Francisco, alleging some schools may be giving minority students an unlawful edge, according to Bloomberg Businessweek.

And in sports, Ben Shelton stunned top seed Carlos Alcaraz at the U.S. Open in a five set thriller that didn't finish until 3:33 in the morning, ending Alcaraz's 18 match Grand Slam winning streak.

blocks.title: Tariffs, Oil Shock and Manitoba's Tax Backdrop for Advisors
blocks.script:
The biggest story on every feed this morning is trade, and it will shape client calls all week. Canada's counter-tariffs against the United States took effect at one minute past midnight, hitting roughly 27.6 billion dollars of American imports with duties running from 15 to 50 percent, per Investment Executive. Wealth Professional puts the retaliation at more than 700 US product lines, dollar for dollar, with no talks scheduled. The direction is what matters here: this is retaliation, not a pause.

Layer an oil shock on top of that. Attacks on energy facilities around the Persian Gulf pushed Brent crude toward 100 US dollars a barrel, the Globe and Mail's Before the Bell reports, with Brent near 98.72 and West Texas Intermediate near 94.04, both up sharply. Goldman Sachs is now floating a 120 dollar scenario if the Strait of Hormuz disruption drags on, according to Wealth Professional. For your clients, that is an inflation input landing right when the rate path looked settled, so keep the Bank of Canada's next decision on your watch list. Investment Executive's own opinion page calls the bond sell off "a repricing of the cost of capital," and that is not a market that shrugs off an oil spike.

Prime Minister Carney is already framing the cost publicly, warning of tough times as the retaliatory tariffs kick in and that the pivot away from the US will come at a cost before it pays off, per Investment Executive. For business owner clients with US exposure, that is a conversation to start now, not after a client calls you worried.

On regulation, three items to flag. Advisor.ca's lead piece today asks what the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization's incoming chief executive needs to deliver: real evidence that self-regulation is working, with changes where it is not. Separately, a rep has been fined and banned by a CIRO hearing panel after admitting to unauthorized transfers, a reminder to keep your own file hygiene tight. And the one worth remembering if a client ever threatens to sue a regulator: the Ontario Superior Court has thrown out a 47.5 million dollar lawsuit against the Mutual Fund Dealers Association and the Ontario Securities Commission, brought by a rep named Valery Herner. The court found no real evidence behind the claims and ruled that a self-regulatory organization does not owe individual reps a duty of care, because that would conflict with its duty to the public. Also on the regulatory side, the Canadian Securities Administrators published a report flagging KYC hurdles and gaps between securities data rules and the federal open banking framework, per Wealth Professional, worth watching if your dealer is touching client data systems this year.

Now to home turf. Manitoba's 2026 budget, tabled by Finance Minister Adrien Sala, made no changes to the corporate income tax rates or the CA$500,000 small-business limit, and no changes to personal income tax rates or tax bracket thresholds. That is the number that matters for your incorporated professional and physician clients: the small business math around active versus passive income holds steady this year. The budget did remove retail sales tax from additional food and beverages sold by grocery stores and prenatal vitamins, effective July 1, 2026, and it raises the renters and homeowners credits starting in 2027. But indexation of Manitoba's tax bracket thresholds to inflation continues to be paused for the 2026 tax year, which quietly pushes more client income into higher brackets over time even without a headline rate change. Worth mentioning at your next incorporated-client review.

On registered accounts, the TFSA dollar limit for 2026 is $7,000, the third year running at that level. The RRSP contribution limit for 2026, subject to any adjustments, is $33,810. The First Home Savings Account limits are unchanged again this year, so if you have a client in a life transition, buying a first home, separating, or relocating, the same annual and lifetime caps still apply and are worth revisiting. On the RESP side, MoneySense has a piece out today making the case that even a late RESP start still captures meaningful grant and growth benefit, a good one to forward to any client who just became a parent or grandparent and assumes they have missed the window.

On product and industry moves: IG Wealth Management has handed its core portfolio mandates to Goldman Sachs Asset Management, which now runs five IG funds and adds its own flagship strategies, Wealth Professional reports. The Canadian ETF market is closing in on 924 billion dollars in assets, with bond funds driving 3.9 billion in inflows in a single week, and autocallable ETFs are being called the next income frontier. Questrade rolled out direct links for an agentic AI trading tool, part of a broader automation push across the discount channel, so expect client questions about it.

On people moves, Investment Executive's industry column flags appointments at RBC, Nicola Wealth and Hub International, plus former ING chief executive Ralph Hamer joining Scotiabank's board, worth noting given Scotia Wealth Management sits inside that group and is on your watch list.

One more for your insurance conversations. Advisor.ca reports that life insurance licensing requirements vary widely across the country, with seven jurisdictions carrying no continuing education requirement at all, while errors and omissions coverage, sponsorship and fees differ province to province. If you have clients with corporate-owned policies structured through an out of province advisor, that patchwork is worth a second look, especially for incorporated professionals using insurance as part of their passive income and estate strategy.
talkingPoints: Manitoba's budget held small business tax rates steady, so your incorporated and physician clients see no surprise change to the passive income math this year.
The Bank of Canada's next rate call is now tangled up with an oil shock, watch that decision closely before locking in fixed income moves.
A court just confirmed self-regulators don't owe individual reps a duty of care, useful context if a client asks about regulatory risk.
TFSA room is 7,000 dollars again for 2026, RRSP room is 33,810 dollars, good hooks for year-end planning calls starting now.
IG Wealth just outsourced its core funds to Goldman Sachs, a sign of where fee and manufacturing pressure in this industry is heading.

blocks.title: Storms, Tariffs, Hydro Hearings, and City Finances
blocks.script:
Manitoba Hydro crews are still working to restore power to the last customers in River Heights, three days after a storm tore through that neighbourhood Sunday night. Winnipeg Free Press reporting describes downed power lines, toppled Hydro poles, and trees crashed onto homes and vehicles, worst around Borebank and Lindsay streets. Nobody was hurt, but CBC reports some residents were still without power going into Wednesday, and the city set up a reception centre at a River Heights community centre. If you have clients with storm damage or business interruption claims in that pocket of the city, this is the week those calls come in.

The bigger economic story is the trade war. Canada's retaliatory tariffs on American goods took effect just after midnight Tuesday, hitting close to twenty billion dollars in United States goods, from sunscreen to dairy, according to the Canadian Press. That's Ottawa's answer to the fifty per cent tariffs Washington put on nearly twenty eight billion dollars of Canadian goods back on August 22nd. Trump escalated again Tuesday, signing orders to ban imports of Canadian alcohol, motorcycles, and other products starting September 29th. Prime Minister Mark Carney told Canadians to expect tough times ahead as the country pivots away from the U.S. Economists quoted by the Canadian Press say grocery bills are largely spared, though health and beauty products could see price bumps. Locally, the Free Press reports Manitoba is stepping up interprovincial trade missions and export loan supports for businesses, though the province's own brewers are questioning how effective that plan will be.

On interest rates: the Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at two and a quarter per cent on September 2nd, the seventh straight hold. The bank said upside risks to inflation have increased while new tariffs make growth prospects more uncertain. That's the backdrop for any client asking why borrowing costs aren't moving despite all the tariff noise. This is on the watch list, and the next decision isn't until late October.

Manitoba Hydro is also in the news for its own reasons. Six weeks of public hearings into Manitoba Hydro's generating plans wrapped up with more criticism of the Crown corporation's proposed natural gas expansion in Brandon, as the Public Utilities Board scrutinized a plan to add 1,760 megawatts of capacity, more than a quarter of the utility's existing generation. That includes a three billion dollar plan to add three gas turbines to the two already running in Brandon. The board now writes a report for cabinet, so no rate decision yet, but expect this to shape Hydro's capital spending, and its borrowing, for years. Manitoba Hydro is on the watch list this morning for that reason alone.

Closer to city hall, Winnipeg is tracking toward a twenty nine million dollar operating shortfall this year, based on June numbers, per CBC. A city councillor is downplaying it publicly, but it's worth having on your radar if you sit on any board watching municipal borrowing or property tax pressure.

In health care, the Manitoba Labour Board has ordered striking Dynacare lab workers back on the job. Roughly 350 technologists and technicians had walked out over wages before the board's ruling. The union isn't happy, but some non-urgent diagnostic testing delays are already built in for the next couple of weeks. Meanwhile the Dauphin Regional Health Centre emergency department reopened Monday, restoring 24 hour emergency service after a two month closure from flood damage, though full hospital services aren't back yet.

On education, two data points worth knowing. An international assessment shows Manitoba students with a small uptick in science but weaker reading and math scores, mirroring a national decline over two decades. At the same time, the Free Press reports independent school enrolment is hitting record levels, now about 12 per cent of students outside the public system, up from 7 per cent in 2000, as more families pay for faith based or alternative schooling.

And on the Jets: goaltender Connor Hellebuyck was a notable no show at the team's pre training camp skate this week, per the Free Press. Nothing official yet on why, but it's the kind of thing that'll come up at the dinner table before it comes up in your meetings.
talkingPoints: The trade war is now two way, and it's hitting specific goods, not groceries broadly, at least for now.

River Heights storm damage and the Dynacare strike back to work order are both live issues for insurance and health care conversations this week.

blocks.title: Tariffs Escalate, Rates Hold, Manitoba Returns
blocks.script:
You need to know where the trade war stands, because it moved fast in the last 24 hours. Canada's counter-tariffs on roughly 28 billion dollars of American goods took effect Tuesday. Within hours, President Trump signed three new proclamations hitting back, expanding Section 338 tariffs to cover Canadian alcohol, non-alcoholic beer, motorcycles, dairy products, and molasses, effective September 29. A U.S. administration official briefing reporters put the value of those new bans in the single digit billions, according to Politico's Canada Playbook. Federal minister Dominic LeBlanc, who holds the Canada-U.S. trade file, said Ottawa is assessing the move and that protecting workers, farmers, and businesses comes first. He says he remains in contact with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. Prime Minister Mark Carney used a video message this week to tell Canadians the pivot away from U.S. trade reliance will be costly, but that the alternative is worse.

Underneath this is the dairy fight. Trump claims Canada shuts out American farmers. But per Politico, U.S. Department of Agriculture data shows American dairy exports to Canada rose 78 percent since the USMCA, the trade deal replacing NAFTA, took effect in 2020, and Agriculture Canada figures put U.S. dairy sales into Canada at 1.31 billion dollars last year against 390 million in Canadian dairy exports the other way. Canada's chief trade negotiator, Janice Charette, told Politico the real sticking point before talks collapsed was American producers not filling quotas they already have, not the quota system itself.

This is on your watch list. The Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at 2.25 percent on September 2. For the seventh time in a row, the central bank told Canadians it would be holding its interest rate steady at 2.25%. The bank pointed to the Middle East conflict keeping energy prices high, plus the new U.S. tariffs and Canadian countermeasures, as sources of ongoing uncertainty. The Globe and Mail's markets desk reports Brent crude pushed close to 100 US dollars a barrel this week after attacks on Gulf energy facilities, another input the bank is watching on the inflation side.

Closer to home: the Manitoba legislature has been on summer break since June 1 and comes back September 29. The House adjourned on June 1, 2026, and the 3rd Session of the 43rd Legislature will reconvene Tuesday, September 29th, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. That's the same day Trump's new bans on Canadian booze and motorcycles kick in. Premier Wab Kinew's NDP government heads into that session having just raised the monthly rent control exemption threshold to 2,000 dollars starting in the new year, and expanded transitional housing funding under its Your Way Home strategy. On the other side of the aisle, the Progressive Conservative opposition is led by Obby Khan, who's held that role since last year.

On the federal machinery side, worth knowing if clients ask about the investment climate: Politico's Canada Playbook reports Dominic Barton was actually appointed chair of Invest in Canada back on July 16, weeks before the government's public announcement of a leadership shakeup on August 31. The outgoing chief executive, Laurel Broten, left more than a year before her five year term was up, just ahead of a mid-September investment summit in Toronto the agency is helping organize. blocks.script:
The biggest story for you today is the trade war, because it's starting to reshape Canadian energy and climate policy at the same time. Canada's retaliatory tariffs on American goods took effect just after midnight Tuesday, hitting everything from sunscreen to dairy, per Canada's National Observer. Trump responded with new executive orders banning imports of Canadian booze, motorcycles, and some dairy products, escalating further. Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the country Monday night, warning of tough times ahead as retaliation begins, and laying out plans to diversify trade and build more capacity domestically, per the Observer. The Observer's own panel discussion this week framed the real question for you: does this economic shock sideline decarbonization, or does it become the opening to rebuild Canada's energy base at home. Worth watching for any client with cross border manufacturing or energy exposure.

Closer to home, Manitoba Hydro, which is on your watch list. Electricity rates rose 4 percent effective January 1st this year, the first increase after a one year provincial freeze, according to the utility's own filings. A residential customer with electric heat is paying roughly 8 dollars more a month. The Crown corporation says it needs to spend 31 billion dollars over the next two decades on aging infrastructure and new generating capacity, partly because two straight years of drought hit hydro revenues, and partly because population growth, electrification, and new data centres are pushing demand up faster than supply. Hydro's own numbers put its debt at 24.6 billion dollars. For clients holding Manitoba Hydro bonds, or watching the province's fiscal picture, that debt load is the thing to track.

On the charity side, three changes landed this year that matter for clients running foundations or private charitable structures. First, the Canada Revenue Agency has added new fields to the T3010 information return specifically to catch foundations that consistently under-disburse against the 5 percent disbursement quota on invested assets, according to Charity Law Group. If a client's foundation hasn't run that calculation properly lately, this is the year to do it. Second, the CRA ended fax filing entirely as of April 1st. Everything now goes through the My Business Account portal, and the agency wants all T3010 returns filed online starting in 2027. Third, in May the CRA issued new guidance on how charities can draft their charitable purposes, but it also confirmed the Charities Directorate no longer offers pre-approval or advance review of proposed changes, according to Philanthropic Foundations Canada. That shifts more of the risk onto a charity's own legal advice before it acts, not after.

On philanthropy trends, The Philanthropist Journal has two pieces worth knowing about today. One asks whether charitable gaming, the 50/50 draws that fund hospital foundations and other causes, is really a win for donors and charities or just a new dependency, a fair question as more organizations lean on it for revenue. The other is from Anita Khanna at United Way slash Centraide Canada, the national federation that includes United Way Winnipeg, which is on your watch list. She argues the nonprofit care workforce is essential infrastructure and needs to be funded and treated that way, given labour shortages across the sector.

And in Alberta, Grassy Mountain, the coal mine Ottawa rejected once already, is back with a scaled-down proposal from Gina Rinehart's Northback Holdings, a reminder that resource approvals keep testing the line between provincial ambition and federal environmental review, and one more data point for clients weighing exposure to Canadian coal and mining names.

blocks.title: Math Feud, Token Theft, and Meta's New Agent
blocks.script:
The biggest technology story overnight is a fight over who actually solved one of the hardest problems in mathematics, and it matters less for the fluid dynamics than for what it shows about how frontier labs behave under pressure.

OpenAI says an internal model, described as significantly more capable than its current Astra system, produced a full proof of the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of seven Millennium Prize problems carrying a one million dollar bounty, and that the underlying question had gone unresolved for roughly ninety years. But NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster says he and Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge were closing in on a related piece of the puzzle, and that OpenAI moved after rumors of their progress reached the company, according to Fortune. Fortune also reports Buckmaster's more serious allegation: that an OpenAI researcher offered him a deal, either publish jointly while OpenAI claimed the full solution, or publish alone but only if he stripped Alpöge's name from the paper because of his Anthropic affiliation. OpenAI denies wrongdoing. In its own release, the company says it began the effort on September first after hearing a rumor, and that it never saw the pair's work through any means before public release, with no user data accessed to solve the problem. Axios reports the compute bill ran into the millions of dollars, with roughly ten thousand agents working the problem at once. For you, the takeaway isn't the math. It's that labs are now racing each other on signals picked up from user conversations, which should make any client typing proprietary or personal detail into these tools pause.

Closer to home for security, Anthropic has confirmed hackers are using infostealer malware, the kind that quietly harvests saved passwords and login sessions, to hijack Claude accounts and drain paid usage without ever touching a password, TechCrunch reports. One affected user only noticed because his account kept consuming tokens on a day he wasn't working. Anthropic signed compromised users out, invalidated sessions, and issued refunds, but told at least one user it couldn't determine how the access happened in the first place. If your clients or staff use any AI subscription, this is the same advice as always: unique passwords, a password manager, and skepticism about anything you download.

Meta launched a personal AI agent called Muse that wants access to email, calendars, payments, and health services, TechCrunch reports, making it Meta's biggest consumer AI bet yet and a real test of whether people trust the company with that much access.

On the money side, Cognition, the AI coding company, hit a forty eight billion dollar valuation, per TechCrunch, a sign investors think AI coding tools won't be winner take all. French lab Mistral raised three billion euros at a twenty one billion euro valuation led partly by Samsung, underlining how "sovereign AI" outside the big American labs is becoming serious business. And Google Cloud struck a deployment deal with Accenture as it tries to catch up in enterprise AI rollouts, a reminder that the productivity gains everyone talks about still depend on unglamorous integration work.

On the Canadian side, BetaKit has a new rundown of how every province and territory is regulating data centres, worth a look if any client has exposure to that build-out.

blocks.title: Climbing for Mental Health, Rinks Under Scrutiny
blocks.script:
The strongest fitness story out there today is really a mental health story, and it is worth folding into any talk about training. Outside Online covers a new German trial comparing structured bouldering therapy against a newer talk therapy called WISE-T, which stands for What's Important: Schedule and Engage Therapy. That therapy focuses on identifying what actually matters to a person and following through on it, instead of just reacting to whatever feels urgent.

Each bouldering session followed the same structure: climbing moderate heights up to ten feet without ropes, thick pads breaking any falls, and each session built around a mindfulness exercise beforehand, the climbing itself, then a relaxation component at the end. The headline result: both the talk therapy and the bouldering therapy cut anxiety scores significantly compared with standard care, which barely moved.

This is not a one-off finding. It builds on earlier randomized trials from the same German research group. In one of those, a hundred and thirty-three outpatients with depression were split between bouldering therapy and a home exercise program, and the bouldering group showed a significantly greater reduction in depressive symptoms, moving from moderate to mild severity, with a Cohen's d of zero point seven seven. That is a meaningfully large effect size for a mental health intervention. The caveat, and it matters: this newest study took place in one city, at one gym, with participants who were employed and already receiving some treatment for anxiety or depression. Small, single-site, not yet something to build a program around, but promising and consistent with prior randomized work.

Practical takeaway if you already lift: climbing adds real-time problem solving and motor learning that repetitive gym work does not, so think of it as a mental health complement to strength training, not a replacement.

On the Canadian health system side, CBC reports that a trio of Calgary parents co-authored a new article in the Canadian Medical Association Journal raising awareness about carbon monoxide exposure in ice rinks after their children were sickened during a tournament nearly two years ago. More than twenty young players fell ill in that 2024 incident, and parents along with health experts are now pushing for mandatory carbon monoxide detectors in all rinks. CTV notes federal guidance recommends the devices but does not require them. Health Canada's own numbers put this in context: over two thousand indoor ice arenas operate across the country, and the resurfacers and edgers used on the ice are typically powered by internal combustion engines that emit carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide. Worth knowing if you or clients spend time in rec facilities, arenas are common ground for training, coaching kids, or just staying active in winter.

blocks.script:
The Globe and Mail has a piece today on why kids get distracted in class, and the message is calming: the fix is easier than parents assume, small changes to routines, not a phone ban. That tracks with Canadian Paediatric Society guidance for younger kids: screen time for children younger than 2 years is not recommended, while screen time for children aged 2 to 5 should be limited to one hour or less per day. Build the habit early, because attention regulation is easier to shape in a toddler than to retrofit in a ten-year-old.

Starting this month, the CCB will provide families with up to $8,157 per child under the age of six and up to $6,883 per child aged six to 17. This represents an increase of up to $160 per child under age six and up to $135 per child aged six to 17 compared with last year. If households made less than $38,237, they would be entitled to the maximum benefit amount for each child with no reductions, with the amount clawed back above that.

The CCB increase gives some families more room to redirect into that RESP.

blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: Income statement top to bottom: revenue recognition and where the judgment lives / RRSP: contribution room, the deduction decision, and withdrawal timing
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Statement forensics, lesson 1: Income statement top to bottom: revenue recognition and where the judgment lives.

The biggest story in accounting fraud is not that companies inflate profit, it is that they inflate revenue, because every line below it depends on that number. Securities and Exchange Commission enforcement data going back over two decades shows revenue recognition as the single most common driver of financial restatements, ahead of expense misclassification, ahead of tax issues.

Here is where the judgment actually sits. Under the current standard, ASC 606, Accounting Standards Codification Topic 606, a company answers four questions before it can book a dollar of revenue: what did I promise to deliver, what is the total price, how do I split that price across each promise, and when does control of that promise pass to the customer. That last question, point in time versus over time, is where most of the discretion lives.

Take Under Armour. In 2015 and 2016 the company pulled forward wholesale shipments in the final days of each quarter to hit growth targets it had guided to Wall Street. Revenue looked fine on the surface, but receivables and retailer inventory grew faster than sales. The SEC investigated, and in 2021 Under Armour paid 9 million dollars to settle the charges without admitting or denying wrongdoing. The revenue was real. The timing was the problem.

The one mistake most people make is reading the revenue growth figure and stopping there. Check it against accounts receivable growth on the balance sheet. If receivables grow faster than revenue for two consecutive quarters, that is not proof of fraud, it is a flag that earnings quality needs a second look. On Thomson ONE, pull this from the financials tab, income statement and balance sheet side by side, matching fiscal periods.

Your task today: open one 10-K you know well, find the revenue recognition footnote, and write down which performance obligations are listed as point in time versus over time. Then compare two years of receivables growth against two years of revenue growth. Fifteen minutes, no more.

What this reveals is where a company's discretion lives inside a rule. What it cannot tell you is whether that discretion was used honestly. That question is exactly what pulls you into the balance sheet and the cash flow statement before you ever touch a chart.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 3: RRSP: contribution room, the deduction decision, and withdrawal timing.

Here is the one number that trips up almost every incorporated business owner: RRSP room is built on earned income, and earned income means salary, not dividends. If your corporation pays you entirely in dividends, you generate zero new RRSP room that year. This catches doctors and business owners constantly, because dividends are often the tax-efficient way to pull money out, but they build no retirement room at all.

The formula is 18 percent of last year's earned income, up to the annual maximum, plus any unused room carried forward. For 2025, the dollar cap is 32,490 dollars. So if a business owner paid themselves a 150,000 dollar salary in 2025, they generate 18 percent of that, which is 27,000 dollars, well under the cap, added to their room for 2026.

Now the part most people skip: contributing and deducting are two separate decisions. You can put money into the RRSP this year and hold the deduction for a future year when your income, and your marginal rate, is higher. In Manitoba, the combined federal and provincial top rate for 2025 sits at 50.40 percent on income over 246,752 dollars. Deducting at that rate versus deducting at 30 percent is a completely different result for the same dollar contributed.

The mistake I see most: people deduct the contribution in the same year they take a sabbatical or parental leave, when income is already low, and they waste the tax value permanently. Once claimed, you can't reclaim that deduction later at a better rate.

On withdrawal timing, the RRSP must convert to a Registered Retirement Income Fund, an RRIF, by the end of the year you turn 71. That rule hasn't changed. But before that deadline, look for low-income years, between jobs, early retirement before pension starts, and pull RRSP money out then, taxed at a lower bracket than working years.
talkingPoints: Company & Economy Analysis: Open one 10-K, find the revenue recognition footnote, note point-in-time versus over-time obligations, then compare two years of receivables growth to two years of revenue growth.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull your 2025 Notice of Assessment, find your RRSP deduction limit on it, and write down whether this year's contribution should be deducted now or carried forward based on where your income is trending.

blocks.label: Markets & Economy
blocks.title: Oil Nears $100 as Trade War, Bond Selloff Deepen
blocks.script:
Good morning. Markets are absorbing a wave of pressure this week from the Middle East, from a widening Canada-US trade fight, and from a global bond selloff that traders say could get "funky" in the months ahead.

Start with oil. Brent crude pushed back toward the 100-dollar-a-barrel mark after the United States and Iran traded tanker attacks over the weekend, and Saudi Arabia said operations were halted at several energy facilities in the kingdom's south following what officials linked to Houthi attacks, according to Bloomberg and The Globe and Mail. WTI crude also jumped sharply. Goldman Sachs has warned crude could surge as high as 120 dollars a barrel if attacks on shipping intensify further.

There was some relief in the numbers, though. Iran said a deal with Oman to manage shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is only days away, and empty Qatari LNG tankers were reported heading back toward the Persian Gulf, a signal that exports may resume. Oil briefly erased its gains on that news before commodity markets more broadly kept marching higher, with copper touching a record and European natural gas prices near a three-year high.

Analysts say the risk premium is doing most of the work in oil right now. Tim Waterer of KCM Trade told the Globe and Mail that tanker flows through Hormuz remain well below normal, and that prices are likely to stay elevated as long as the strait remains contested and diplomacy stays fragile.

On trade, Canada's retaliatory tariffs on roughly 28 billion dollars of American goods took effect today, hitting nearly 700 products with duties of 15, 25 or 50 percent, according to the Globe and Mail. Industrial goods like aluminum, steel, cardboard and screws bear the brunt, though clothing, furniture, dairy and cosmetics are also affected. Prime Minister Mark Carney used a national address to warn Canadians that the pivot away from the United States will come at a cost, but argued the alternative would be worse.

The Trump administration is expected to escalate further this week. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has confirmed plans for additional tariffs on Canadian goods, potentially including outright import bans. Over the past two days Donald Trump has also threatened to bar US sales of Bombardier jets unless production moves to America, a threat that has already knocked down Bombardier shares.

Bond markets are under their own strain. Yields on longer-dated debt in France, Italy and the UK have risen faster than anywhere else in the G7 over the past month, hitting multi-year highs, as Europe's energy exposure comes back into focus. Allianz economist Ludovic Subran said higher inflation expectations have shifted anticipated central bank policy rates upward, a major driver of the move in longer-dated yields. Gas prices have climbed more than 120 percent since the start of the Iran war.

The US 10-year Treasury yield was last near 4.8 percent. Deutsche Bank strategist Henry Allen argues markets are underestimating how much central banks will ultimately need to raise rates given current price pressures, framing it simply: either inflation falls, or the pressure on rates continues.

Despite all this, stocks have shown resilience. Bloomberg notes that credit spreads remain tight and companies don't appear rattled by current borrowing costs, especially with earnings growing more than 20 percent year on year in some cases, according to Collin Martin at the Schwab Center for Financial Research. Still, JPMorgan has flagged sharply deteriorating liquidity in the Treasury market, even if that stress hasn't spread meaningfully to stock futures or corporate bond funds.

Currency markets delivered one of the bigger surprises. The Japanese yen surged to its strongest level since February, breaking through 155 per dollar and triggering stop-losses that accelerated the move, according to Bloomberg. That has forced investors to unwind an estimated 2.35 trillion dollars in yen-funded carry trades. Japan's finance minister said the currency stance is unchanged from the earlier period of coordinated intervention with Washington.

In China, authorities are injecting 45 billion dollars into the country's largest banks and insurers to bolster the financial system as growth slows, though shares of some of those insurers and banks fell on fears the recapitalization will dilute existing shareholders.

Corporate news included a rough stretch for Novartis. The Swiss drugmaker's shares fell sharply, at one point reported down as much as 10 percent, after its heart medicine del-desiran failed a final-stage study, its second or third clinical setback within a single week depending on the count. The failure also hit shares of Ionis Pharmaceuticals, which had licensed the drug to Novartis, along with other biotech names.

Elsewhere, ZIM Integrated Shipping rose after reports that Hapag-Lloyd and FIMI plan to raise their takeover offer for the container shipping company. And Goldman Sachs strategist Timothy Moe reaffirmed his bullish call on South Korean stocks, keeping a Kospi target of 12,000 on the view that investors are underestimating how long an AI-driven boost to memory chipmakers will last.

Looking ahead, the European Central Bank is widely expected to deliver a rate increase on Thursday, with attention on whether officials leave the door open to a third hike later this year. In the US, producer and consumer price data due later in the week will be closely watched ahead of the Federal Reserve's meeting later this month, with markets pricing rate-hike bets after a stronger-than-expected jobs report.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Bombardier, Novartis Lead A Trade-War News Cycle
blocks.script:
Start with Bombardier, the Montreal business jet maker now at the center of the Canada-US trade fight. Donald Trump posted on Truth Social Monday that NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren't good enough, unless the company builds there, hours before Canada's measures, covering 27.6 billion dollars in US imports at rates of 15%, 25% and 50%, applied from 00:01 on September 8, 2026. The tailwind: Bombardier's jets are FAA certified and USMCA compliant, and an aerospace analyst said he did not believe any business jet customers would cancel Bombardier orders and didn't see how Trump could stop them from being sold. The headwind: the move drew an objection hours later from Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., whose state hosts Bombardier's U.S. headquarters. An advisor tells a client: price the fundamentals, not the Truth Social post.

Novartis, the Swiss pharma giant, just took its third clinical trial hit within a week. Bloomberg's markets newsletter reports shares slumped as much as 10 percent after del-desiran, a drug from a recent acquisition, failed a late-stage study, following an earlier heart-medicine disappointment. The tailwind: the balance sheet is large enough to absorb one bad quarter. The headwind: Ionis Pharmaceuticals, which licensed the failed drug, fell 11 percent in premarket trading, and Bloomberg notes Dyne Therapeutics dropped 34 percent, Sarepta 16 percent, and Amgen 5.5 percent in sympathy, dragging the whole biotech complex lower. An advisor says: one trial readout is exactly why you diversify across a sector, not a stock.

Enbridge, the Calgary pipeline giant, announced a leadership change. The Globe and Mail reports Michele Harradence, currently head of its gas distribution and storage business, becomes the next CEO as Greg Ebel retires. The tailwind: an internal successor signals continuity, at a moment the Globe says oil patch merger activity, including Shell's ARC Resources deal, is booming on confidence in Canada's gas export strategy. The headwind: any CEO transition carries execution risk inside a capital-intensive network exposed to tariff and energy-price swings. An advisor says: don't trade the succession headline, watch the next guidance update instead.

Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, walked away from a deal. Bloomberg reports it explored acquiring startup Decart AI for about six billion dollars, did the due diligence, then backed out. The tailwind: Anthropic is reportedly seeking to raise as much in its own initial public offering as SpaceX has, underlining investor appetite. The headwind: walking from a six billion dollar deal after diligence raises questions about acquisition discipline in a frothy AI market, where Bloomberg also notes rival Mistral just raised three billion euros at a valuation above twenty-one billion. An advisor says: private AI stakes are a speculative sleeve, not a core holding.

Apple is testing a new hardware category. The Globe and Mail reports device lead John Ternus faces an AI test with the launch of a new foldable iPhone and a Siri overhaul. The tailwind: the Globe cites analysts saying the foldable could emerge as a category leader despite its price. The headwind: Siri has lagged competitors for years, and a hefty price tag risks limiting the device to a niche audience rather than driving a broad upgrade cycle. An advisor says: Apple's valuation already assumes strong execution, so this launch needs to beat expectations, not just meet them.

Tamarack Valley and Headwater, two Alberta oil producers, agreed to merge. The Globe and Mail reports the ten billion dollar deal creates the largest publicly traded producer focused on the Clearwater formation. The tailwind: it lands inside what the Globe calls an oil patch merger boom, following Shell's ARC Resources purchase, a vote of confidence in Western Canada's export strategy. The headwind: integrating two producers brings execution risk just as Brent crude pushes back toward one hundred dollars on Middle East tension. An advisor says: energy consolidation plays are a sector bet, size the position like one.

Huawei, the Chinese telecom equipment giant, heads to a US courtroom. The Globe and Mail reports jury selection begins this week, eight years after prosecutors charged the company with defrauding HSBC and other banks over its Iran business dealings. The tailwind: Huawei has kept growing in markets outside Washington's reach despite years of sanctions. The headwind: the trial keeps US-China tech tension in headlines just as chip export restrictions tighten further. An advisor says: Huawei isn't investable for most Canadian clients anyway, so treat this as geopolitical signal, not portfolio news.

ASML, the Dutch maker of chipmaking machines, is riding the AI buildout. Bloomberg reports it has won commitments from top chipmakers to use its latest production gear, part of a broader push to meet surging demand as supply chains get remade. The tailwind: it holds a near monopoly on the extreme ultraviolet lithography every advanced chipmaker needs. The headwind: that same AI buildout is pushing corporate borrowing to record levels, adding upward pressure on bond yields that could eventually cool capital spending. An advisor says: ASML is a genuine quality compounder, but priced for a lot of good news.

IG Wealth Management, the Winnipeg-based advisor overseeing savings for roughly one million Canadians, made a notable hire. The Globe and Mail reports it's brought in Goldman Sachs to bring institutional investment strategy to retail clients. The tailwind: a Manitoba-headquartered firm borrowing the same playbook big pensions use could narrow the gap between retail and institutional returns. The headwind: institutional strategies often carry fees and complexity that don't always translate cleanly into individual accounts. An advisor says: ask exactly what changes in your portfolio, not just whose name is now attached to the strategy.

Sigma Lithium, the Canadian-listed lithium miner with Brazilian operations, hit a legal snag. Bloomberg reports shares dropped 11 percent after a Brazilian court ordered a halt to mining at its Grota do Cirilo project, though the company says its operations remain unaffected pending appeal. The tailwind: global lithium demand tied to electrification stays structurally intact. The headwind: single-jurisdiction regulatory risk just turned real, and courts move faster than press releases. An advisor says: commodity miners operating in emerging jurisdictions carry exactly the kind of headline risk a diversified fund is built to absorb.

On the rest of your watch list: the Bank of Canada isn't back until October 28, it held its rate steady this month, flagging tariffs as an upside inflation risk, that's the backdrop for every trade-war story above but it's outside our 48 hour window. Dimensional Fund Advisors, Scotia Wealth Management, Manitoba Hydro, United Way Winnipeg, the Jets and the Blue Bombers drew no coverage in business or markets news over the period.
